ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Measles is a highly contagious RNA virus causing fever, rash and immune suppression. Diagnosis relies on clinical triad and serology; management centers on supportive care and vitamin A. Prompt care prevents severe complications.

sections.p: Measles is an acute, highly contagious viral infection caused by a paramyxovirus. Classic presentation includes fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a maculopapular rash that starts at the hairline and spreads downward.
b: Incubation 10–14 days; rash appears 3–5 days after fever onset

t.b: Detects recent infection; positive IgM confirms acute disease
Confirms diagnosis when serology unavailable or in early disease
Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia are typical; normal counts may mislead

sections.p: Severity is graded by the presence of complications and organ involvement. The WHO severity scale ranges from uncomplicated to severe with pneumonia, encephalitis or death.
b: Severe: pneumonia, otitis media, encephalitis, or death

sections.p: Primary cause is measles virus infection. In low‑resource settings, secondary bacterial pneumonia, malnutrition, HIV co‑infection, and vitamin A deficiency increase severity.
Patients develop a prodrome of fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, followed by Koplik spots and a spreading rash. Complications include pneumonia, otitis media, diarrhea, and encephalitis.
b: Rash: maculopapular, starts at hairline, spreads to trunk and limbs

sections.p: Investigations confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and rule out mimics. In resource‑limited settings, clinical criteria may suffice.

t.b: Leukopenia indicates viral infection; normal counts may miss early disease
Detects pneumonia; absence does not rule out early pulmonary involvement
Positive confirms measles; negative early in course may be false negative

sections.p: Urgent complications require immediate care: severe pneumonia, dehydration, seizures, and encephalitis. Red flags include high fever >40 °C, persistent vomiting, altered consciousness, and severe respiratory distress.
b: Severe rash with bullae – risk of secondary infection

sections.p: Supportive care is the mainstay. Vitamin A is essential to reduce mortality. Antipyretics, hydration, and monitoring are mandatory. Antibiotics are reserved for secondary bacterial infections.
b: Vaccination – MMR for contacts and outbreak control

sections.p: Post‑infection, monitor for bronchiectasis and immune suppression. Prevention relies on vaccination, cold chain maintenance, and vitamin A supplementation in endemic areas.
Measles can be mistaken for rubella, varicella, and scarlet fever. Key distinguishing features are Koplik spots, rash distribution, and prodrome severity.
b: Scarlet fever – sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue

sections.p: Early serology may be negative; normal CBC can occur early. Chest X‑ray may miss early pneumonia. Vitamin A levels may be falsely low due to malnutrition.
b: Chest X‑ray normal in early viral pneumonia

faq.q: Why is vitamin A given to all measles patients?
faq.a: It reduces mortality, prevents blindness, and supports immune function.

faq.q: Can measles be transmitted after the rash appears?
faq.a: Yes, patients are contagious from 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset.

faq.q: What is the role of the cold chain for measles vaccine?
faq.a: Measles vaccine must be stored 2–8 °C; freezing destroys potency.
